title: Preparing for and explaining in discussions
keyIdea: A good discussion starts before anyone speaks. Read the text and make short notes: a fact, a question and your view with a reason. In the talk, back your points by naming the fact and where it came from, so others can check it. Ask open questions that start with how or why. At the end, explain your thinking: what you thought at first, what someone pointed out, and what you think now and why.
familyTip: Before a family chat about a plan, like where to go at the weekend, give everyone one fact to look up. Each person brings a fact, a question and their view with a reason. Afterwards, take turns to finish the sentence: At first I thought..., but then... pointed out..., so now I think...

visual.caption: Which notes would help you in a discussion about the school garden? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Fact 1: 40 kg of potatoes for lunches
The whole fact sheet copied out

lab.caption: Flagship lab: pack notes, back points with facts, reply by pointing to the text, ask open questions, explain a change of mind.

kid: Before a discussion, get ready. Read what you were given. Then write a few short notes, not the whole text.
Good notes have three parts. A fact you can use. A question you want to ask. Your view, with a reason that starts with because.
When you speak, point to your notes. Say which fact, and where it came from. Fact 1 says the garden grew 40 kg of potatoes. Now everyone can check it.

Ask open questions that start with how or why. They get people talking. A yes or no question can stop the talk. At the end, say what you think now. It is fine to change your mind. Say what you thought, what changed it, and why.
adult: Ages 8 to 11. The US Common Core asks pupils in grades 4 and 5 to come to discussions prepared, to draw on that preparation and other known facts, to ask and answer specific questions, and to explain their own ideas in light of the discussion (SL.4.1 and SL.5.1). In England, the KS2 spoken language strand asks pupils to justify answers and opinions, and to consider and evaluate different viewpoints.

Preparation is a skill, not a chore. Show your child how to turn a text into three short notes: one fact they can quote, one question that has no easy answer, and their own view with a reason. In the talk, the phrase 'Fact 1 says...' or 'The leaflet says...' does more than a louder voice.

Common mistakes: copying the text out word for word instead of picking key points; disagreeing with 'No it isn't!' and no evidence; vague references such as 'I read somewhere'; asking closed yes or no questions that end the talk; and treating a change of mind as losing. Be careful to praise a changed view when your child can say what evidence changed it.

In the lab your child packs notes for a class question about the school garden, backs three points with facts that light up on the fact sheet, replies to three classmates by naming the fact, sorts open and closed questions, and builds a sentence that explains how their thinking changed.

practice.prompt: Five pupils each bring a fact, a question and a view to the discussion. That is 3 notes each. Then {n} more pupils join with 3 notes each. How many notes are there now?
practice.hint: Count the pupils first: 5 and {n} more. Each one has 3 notes.
practice.explain: 5 + {n} = {=5+n} pupils, and 3 notes each makes {=3*(5+n)} notes.

practice.prompt: Your group has 20 minutes to talk. You spend {n} minutes reading the fact sheet first. How many minutes are left for the discussion?
practice.hint: Take the reading time away from the 20 minutes.
practice.explain: 20 take away {n} minutes of reading leaves {=20-n} minutes to talk, and your notes make those minutes count.

practice.prompt: Which note is a view with a reason?
choices: Keep the garden, because we learn to grow food
Keep the garden
The garden is on the field
practice.explain: A view says what you think. The reason after because says why. Keep the garden on its own has no reason, and the last one is a fact.

practice.prompt: Mia says the garden is a waste of time. Which reply points to the text?
choices: Fact 1 says it grew 40 kg of potatoes for our lunches
No it isn't!
I read something about it once
practice.hint: Which reply says what the text says, so Mia can check it?
practice.explain: Naming the fact and where it came from lets everyone check it. The other replies give no evidence.

practice.prompt: Which question will get people talking?
choices: Why do you think the garden matters?
Do you like the garden?
Is the garden big?
practice.hint: Can the question be answered with just yes or no?
practice.explain: Why... is an open question, so people give reasons. The other two are closed: yes or no ends them.

pool.prompt: What should you do before a class discussion about a text?
choices: Read it and note a fact, a question and your view
Copy the whole text out neatly
Nothing, just say what you feel on the day
pool.hint: Which way gives you things you can use while you talk?
pool.explain: Short notes you can use are the point of preparing. Copying everything takes time and is hard to use in the talk.

pool.prompt: Leo says nobody would look after the garden in the holidays. Which reply is best?
choices: Fact 3 says it needs watering 3 times a week, so we could make a rota
That's just not true
I don't know
pool.hint: Which reply uses what you prepared and adds an idea?
pool.explain: It names the fact and builds on it with a plan. Just not true gives no reason.

pool.prompt: Ava thought the garden should close. Then she heard that 25 pupils use it. Now she wants to keep it. What should she say?
choices: At first I thought it should close, but 25 pupils use it, so now I think we should keep it
I was right all along
Nothing, so nobody notices she changed
pool.hint: Explain your thinking: before, what changed it, and now.
pool.explain: Saying what changed your mind shows good thinking. It is not losing.

pool.prompt: Ben says 'It said somewhere that the club is short.' How can he make it stronger?
choices: Say which text and which fact: Fact 2 says it meets for 1 hour
Say it louder
Say it three times
pool.hint: How could the others check what Ben means?
pool.explain: Somewhere is vague. Naming the fact lets everyone look at the same evidence.

pool.prompt: Which is an open question for the discussion?
choices: How could we grow more food next year?
Is it sunny today?
Do you like carrots?
pool.hint: Open questions often start with how or why.
pool.explain: How could we... needs ideas and reasons. The others need only yes or no.

pool.prompt: Which is evidence for the point 'Lots of pupils enjoy the garden'?
choices: Fact 4: 25 pupils are in the garden club
Everyone says so
Fact 1: 40 kg of potatoes for lunches
pool.hint: Which fact is about how many pupils take part?
pool.explain: The number in the club backs up the point. Everyone says so is not evidence, and the potatoes back up a different point.

pool.prompt: You prepared {n} questions. In the discussion you asked 2 of them. How many questions are still in your notes to ask?
pool.hint: Take the 2 you asked away from the {n} you prepared.
pool.explain: {n} take away 2 leaves {=n-2} questions you can still use later in the talk.

pool.prompt: Sam says 'No it isn't!' to every point. What is missing?
choices: A reason or a fact to back him up
A louder voice
Nothing, disagreeing is enough
pool.hint: What would help others see why Sam disagrees?
pool.explain: It is fine to disagree. A reason or a fact from the text makes it worth hearing.

pool.prompt: A group of {n} pupils each make 1 point in the talk, and each point needs 1 fact to back it. How many facts does the group need?
pool.hint: One fact for each point, and one point for each pupil.
pool.explain: {n} points need {n} facts, one behind each point.
